paras: The lynching of Jim Smith was the killing of a Black man by a mob of white men in Crittenden County, Arkansas, in late November 1888. Smith, accused of an offense against a white farmer's wife, was taken from a deputy sheriff on the way to jail at Marion and shot. The case reached readers only through brief wire items in papers outside Arkansas.

According to a Memphis dispatch of November 29, Smith met the wife of a white farmer in the road and made an "insulting proposal" to her. In that account she fled, and he pursued her until the approach of a horseman frightened him away. A shorter item said instead that Smith "assaulted" the woman, and placed the offense on Wednesday, November 28.

After the woman reported what had happened, a deputy sheriff arrested Smith. While the deputy was taking him to the jail at Marion, the two were met by a mob of white men who took the prisoner from the officer. The mob shot Smith to death, filling him "full of bullets" in the Memphis version and "full of buckshot" in the other.
No report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage, and none of the papers named the woman, the deputy or any member of the mob.

The Omaha Daily Bee ran the Memphis dispatch on its front page on November 30 under the headline "An Arkansas Negro Lynched," telling the woman's account as fact and the killing in a single closing clause. The same day the Clarksville Evening Chronicle and the Maysville Evening Bulletin carried a one-sentence version in an identical column of brief items, "Pointed Paragraphs," between notices of a bust unveiling and a postoffice robbery trial. The McCook Tribune in Nebraska reprinted the Memphis text a week later, on December 7.
None of the items questioned the accusation or commented on the mob, and no Arkansas or Memphis paper's own account appears in the coverage.

The two versions differ on the charge: the Memphis dispatch describes an insulting proposal and a chase that ended before Smith reached the woman, while the column item says he "assaulted" her. They also differ on whether the mob used bullets or buckshot; the fuller Memphis dispatch gives the more detailed account of the alleged offense.

reader.title: Lynching of Jim Smith
bases: A mob of white men took Jim Smith, an accused Black man, from a deputy sheriff on the way to jail and shot him to death (A1, A2).
Smith was shot to death by 'a mob of white men' who took him from an officer without any lawful authority, as punishment for an alleged offense against a white farmer's wife (A1, A2).

Two differently worded wire items agree on the core event (A1, A2), but neither is a local report, both ran the same day far from Arkansas, and both likely derive from the same Memphis news (A1 is datelined Memphis); A3 and A4 are reprints.

accounts.label: 'Pointed Paragraphs' news column
accounts.gist: Smith assaulted a white farmer's wife on Wednesday, was arrested soon afterward, and was taken from the officer by a mob of white men and filled with buckshot.

info: The alleged offense was on Wednesday (Nov. 28, 1888, by the date of the paper); the lynching followed 'soon afterward' and was reported from Memphis on Nov. 29.
On the road to the jail at Marion, Crittenden County, Arkansas; no exact spot is given.
Jim Smith, described as 'a negro' and 'a colored man'.
Accused of making an insulting proposal to a white farmer's wife on the road and pursuing her until a horseman approached (A1); another version says he 'assaulted' her (A2).
